title: Tracking Global Greenhouse Gas Emissions
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Human activities release greenhouse gases into the air. These gases trap heat around the Earth and contribute to climate change. Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels like coal, oil, and gas is the main cause. People have increased carbon dioxide levels by about fifty percent since pre-industrial times.
pages.caption: Greenhouse gas emissions per person in the highest-emitting countries (as of 2023). Areas of rectangles represent total emissions for each country.

evidence.fileTitle: File:20210626 Variwide chart of greenhouse gas emissions per capita by country.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Greenhouse gas emissions per person in the highest-emitting countries (as of 2023). Areas of rectangles represent total emissions for each country.

pages.text: Carbon dioxide is the main gas and accounts for more than half of all warming. Methane has a big short-term impact as well. Other gases like nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases play a lesser role. Energy use, including electricity and transport, is responsible for most of these total emissions.
pages.caption: The industrial era growth in atmospheric CO2-equivalent gas concentrations since 1750

pages.text: Industrial activities and factories have grown rapidly since the middle of the twentieth century. Global population and economic activity grew quickly after World War Two. This expansion caused emissions to rise across the world. Power generation and transport remain major sources of these gases.
pages.caption: Per capita CO2 emissions surged after the mid-20th century, but then slowed their rate of growth.

evidence.fileTitle: File:1800- Global carbon dioxide emissions, per person.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Per capita CO2 emissions surged after the mid-20th century, but then slowed their rate of growth.

pages.text: Industrialized countries usually have much higher annual emissions per person than developing nations. People in rich nations often produce up to ten times more than the average in developing countries. China has experienced fast economic development and its emissions per person have increased quickly.
pages.caption: Scaling the effect of wealth to the national level: richer (developed) countries emit more CO2 per person than poorer (developing) countries. Emissions are roughly proportional to GDP per person, though the rate of increase diminishes with average GDP/pp of about $10,000.

pages.text: Experts use carbon footprints to compare how much greenhouse gas is produced by goods or services. This tracking helps people understand the effects of emissions on the climate. Tracking real-time carbon emissions helps scientists monitor sources like power stations and coal mines worldwide.

Greenhouse gas emissions from human activities intensify the natural greenhouse effect, which contributes significantly to global climate change. Carbon dioxide released from burning fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas remains the primary driver. Human activities have increased atmospheric carbon dioxide by about fifty percent over pre-industrial levels.

Methane emissions carry almost the same short-term impact, while nitrous oxide and fluorinated gases play lesser roles. Overall energy production, including electricity generation, heat, and transport, is responsible for roughly seventy-three percent of global emissions.

Emissions then grew rapidly after 1950 alongside expansions in global population and economic activity. The power sector contributes the largest share of total emissions at approximately twenty-seven percent, followed by transport and industry.

pages.text: A carbon footprint serves as an indicator to compare the total greenhouse gases emitted over an entire life cycle, from production to final consumption. Carbon accounting frameworks help measure and track these emissions to understand their impacts on the climate. Independent groups also monitor real-time emissions using satellite data and artificial intelligence.

C1-C2.headline: Dynamics and Accounting of Greenhouse Gases

pages.text: Anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions intensify the atmospheric greenhouse effect, driving contemporary climate change. Combustion of fossil fuels constitutes the primary mechanism, having elevated atmospheric carbon dioxide by approximately fifty percent relative to pre-industrial benchmarks. Historical cumulative emissions reflect substantial contributions from both fossil fuel utilization and land-use changes.
pages.caption: Greenhouse gas emissions per person in the highest-emitting countries (as of 2023). Areas of rectangles represent total emissions for each country.

pages.text: Carbon dioxide represents the principal anthropogenic driver accounting for the majority of surface warming, while methane exerts a nearly equivalent immediate short-term impact. Nitrous oxide and various fluorinated gases contribute comparably minor fractions. Energy sectors, encompassing electricity, thermal generation, and transport, generate the vast majority of total global outputs.

pages.text: Industrial expansion powered by fossil fuels initiated a sustained elevation of atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations beginning around 1750, followed by accelerated growth post-1950 driven by global demographic and economic shifts. Sectoral analyses indicate the power generation domain remains the single largest contributor, followed by transport, industrial energy, and agricultural activities.

pages.text: Disparities in annual per capita emissions remain pronounced, with industrialized economies frequently recording rates up to an order of magnitude higher than developing counterparts. Concurrently, rapid economic development in nations such as China has propelled domestic per capita rates toward parity with traditional developed country groupings.

These indices evaluate supply chain emissions from initial production to final consumption. Advanced monitoring initiatives synthesize satellite observations with artificial intelligence to refine verification protocols for atmospheric carbon and methane.

title: Understanding the 1994 Rwandan Conflict
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The Rwandan genocide happened in 1994. It lasted for about one hundred days. During this time, many people were killed by militias. Most victims were from the Tutsi ethnic group. Some moderate Hutus and Twa people were also killed. The violence was extreme and caused great suffering across the country.
pages.caption: Tutsi murdered by Hutu militia in January 1964

evidence.fileTitle: File:Africa addio (1966) - Rwandan revolution 2.png
evidence.articleCaption: Tutsi murdered by Hutu militia in January 1964

pages.text: The conflict had deep historical roots. In 1990, a civil war started when the Rwandan Patriotic Front invaded from Uganda. A tentative peace happened later, but tensions remained very high. The situation changed dramatically after the president was killed in a plane crash.
pages.caption: Paul Kagame, commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front for most of the Civil War

evidence.fileTitle: File:Paul Kagame 2014.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Paul Kagame, commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front for most of the Civil War

pages.text: During the years before the violence, militias were trained and armed. The radio broadcasted propaganda against the Tutsi group. People were encouraged to view their neighbors with suspicion and fear. This propaganda helped spread hatred throughout the entire country very quickly.
pages.caption: Monogram of Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines

evidence.fileTitle: File:RaTeLiMilCo.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Monogram of Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines

pages.text: The international community failed to stop the terrible killings. The rebel forces eventually defeated the government and ended the genocide. Many people fled to neighboring countries as refugees. This movement of people caused further instability in the wider region.
pages.caption: Juvénal Habyarimana in 1980

evidence.fileTitle: File:Juvénal Habyarimana (1980).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Juvénal Habyarimana in 1980

pages.text: Today, the legacy of the genocide remains very important in Rwanda. The country has created special public holidays to remember the victims. Laws were also passed to prevent future ethnic division and hatred. The nation continues to deal with this tragic history.

The Rwandan genocide was a devastating period of violence that occurred from April to July 1994 during the ongoing civil war. Over a span of approximately one hundred days, members of the Tutsi ethnic group, along with moderate Hutus and Twa, were systematically killed by militias. Scholarly estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of people lost their lives amid widespread atrocities.
pages.caption: Tutsi murdered by Hutu militia in January 1964

evidence.fileTitle: File:Africa addio (1966) - Rwandan revolution 2.png
evidence.articleCaption: Tutsi murdered by Hutu militia in January 1964

pages.text: The origins of the tragedy trace back to long-standing ethnic tensions and earlier conflicts. The Rwandan Civil War began in 1990 when the predominantly Tutsi rebel group invaded from Uganda. Although the Arusha Accords attempted to establish peace in 1993, the assassination of the president on April 6, 1994, ignited the mass violence.
pages.caption: Paul Kagame, commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front for most of the Civil War

evidence.fileTitle: File:Paul Kagame 2014.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Paul Kagame, commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front for most of the Civil War

pages.text: In the years leading up to the crisis, authorities armed civilians and formed paramilitary groups like the Interahamwe. Meanwhile, a popular radio station broadcasted intense anti-Tutsi propaganda. Broadcasters characterized the entire ethnic group as a dangerous threat, effectively preparing the public for the subsequent systematic attacks.
pages.caption: Monogram of Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines

evidence.fileTitle: File:RaTeLiMilCo.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Monogram of Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines

pages.text: Despite the immense scale of the violence, the international community failed to intervene and stop the killings. The rebel forces ultimately defeated the government troops, ending the genocide and prompting the flight of many refugees into neighboring countries, which triggered further regional conflict.
pages.caption: Juvénal Habyarimana in 1980

evidence.fileTitle: File:Juvénal Habyarimana (1980).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Juvénal Habyarimana in 1980

pages.text: The legacy of the genocide continues to influence modern Rwanda significantly. The government has established public commemoration holidays and enacted legislation to criminalize divisionism and genocide ideology. Meanwhile, domestic courts and specialized legal mechanisms were eventually set up to prosecute those responsible for the atrocities.

C1-C2.headline: The Anatomy of the 1994 Rwandan Genocide

pages.text: The Rwandan genocide, recognized as the genocide against the Tutsi, unfolded over approximately one hundred days between April and July 1994 amid the Rwandan Civil War. While official constitutional figures cite over one million fatalities, scholarly consensus estimates that between 500,000 and 662,000 Tutsi were systematically murdered by Hutu militias, accompanied by widespread sexual violence and the targeting of moderate Hutus and Twa.
pages.caption: Tutsi murdered by Hutu militia in January 1964

evidence.fileTitle: File:Africa addio (1966) - Rwandan revolution 2.png
evidence.articleCaption: Tutsi murdered by Hutu militia in January 1964

pages.text: The catastrophe was deeply rooted in historical grievances, including the social shifts of the 1959-1962 Hutu Revolution and the subsequent exile of Tutsis. Hostilities escalated significantly when the Rwandan Patriotic Front invaded from Uganda in 1990. Although the 1993 Arusha Accords offered a tentative peace, the fatal downing of President Juvénal Habyarimana's aircraft on April 6, 1994, served as the immediate catalyst for the genocide.
pages.caption: Paul Kagame, commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front for most of the Civil War

evidence.fileTitle: File:Paul Kagame 2014.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Paul Kagame, commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front for most of the Civil War

pages.text: In the preceding years, the state expanded its military forces and armed civilians under the guise of civil defense. Hutu Power extremists mobilized paramilitary groups, while media outlets such as the RTLM disseminated dehumanizing propaganda that framed the entire Tutsi population as a collective security threat. The extent to which these actions were planned in advance remains a subject of ongoing historical debate and judicial scrutiny.
pages.caption: Monogram of Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines

evidence.fileTitle: File:RaTeLiMilCo.svg
evidence.articleCaption: Monogram of Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines

pages.text: Faced with international inaction and failure to intervene, the RPF resumed military operations and ultimately defeated government forces, capturing state territory to halt the genocide. This victory precipitated the mass exodus of génocidaires and refugees into Zaire, directly contributing to regional destabilization and the outbreak of the First Congo War.
pages.caption: Juvénal Habyarimana in 1980

evidence.fileTitle: File:Juvénal Habyarimana (1980).jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Juvénal Habyarimana in 1980

pages.text: In the aftermath, Rwanda confronted the monumental task of accountability and reconciliation. The RPF government enacted legislation in 1996 to initiate domestic trials for genocide and crimes against humanity, categorizing perpetrators based on their leadership roles and severity of conduct. Today, the legacy of the genocide persists through institutionalized public holidays and strict legislation criminalizing genocide ideology and divisionism.

title: The History and Impact of Anti-Gay Laws
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: In many parts of the world, laws make same-sex acts a crime. These laws are often not used for private acts. However, they can still cause big problems. They lead to unfair treatment, violence, and fear for many people. These laws also make it harder for people to get health care.
pages.caption: "Love is not a crime" signs at Paris Pride 2019

evidence.fileTitle: File:Love is not a crime, Paris Pride 2019.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: "Love is not a crime" signs at Paris Pride 2019

pages.text: Some of these laws come from the British Empire. Other countries use religious laws to punish people. Today, many countries do not have these laws. But in some places, people can still face very harsh punishments, including death, for their sexual acts.
pages.caption: The burning of the knight Richard Puller von Hohenburg with his servant before the walls of Zurich, for sodomy, 1482

evidence.fileTitle: File:Burning of Sodomites.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The burning of the knight Richard Puller von Hohenburg with his servant before the walls of Zurich, for sodomy, 1482

pages.text: Long ago, some societies punished same-sex acts. In the Middle Ages, some European cities made new laws against them. These laws were often used to punish people during times of fear. Sometimes, people were even killed because of these old rules.
pages.caption: Participant carrying a poster against Section 377 during Bhubaneswar Pride Parade, India

evidence.fileTitle: File:Bhubaneswar Pride Parade 2018 02.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Participant carrying a poster against Section 377 during Bhubaneswar Pride Parade, India

pages.text: Today, these laws are hard to enforce because they happen in private. Even when they are not used, they make people feel unsafe. They can lead to police trouble or being treated badly by others. This causes a lot of pain and stress for many people.
pages.caption: Proportion of the world population living in a country where homosexual acts are not criminalized, 1760–2020

evidence.fileTitle: File:Proportion of the world population living in a country where homosexual acts are not criminalized, 1760-2020.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Proportion of the world population living in a country where homosexual acts are not criminalized, 1760–2020

pages.text: Some countries still use fake medical tests to find out if someone is gay. These tests are not real science and are considered torture by the United Nations. Many people around the world are working to change these laws and protect human rights for everyone.

B1-B2.headline: The History and Impact of Anti-Gay Laws

pages.text: Laws criminalizing same-sex acts exist in many regions today. While these laws are frequently unenforced regarding private, consensual conduct, they contribute to significant social harm. They often lead to police harassment, violence, and stigma. Furthermore, these laws discourage people from seeking necessary medical care, which worsens public health issues like HIV.
pages.caption: "Love is not a crime" signs at Paris Pride 2019

evidence.fileTitle: File:Love is not a crime, Paris Pride 2019.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: "Love is not a crime" signs at Paris Pride 2019

pages.text: Many of these legal codes were inherited from the British Empire, which spread such laws to its colonies. Other nations base their laws on religious traditions. While a global wave of decriminalization occurred after World War II, some countries have recently increased enforcement, often citing the false belief that homosexuality is a foreign import.
pages.caption: The burning of the knight Richard Puller von Hohenburg with his servant before the walls of Zurich, for sodomy, 1482

evidence.fileTitle: File:Burning of Sodomites.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: The burning of the knight Richard Puller von Hohenburg with his servant before the walls of Zurich, for sodomy, 1482

pages.text: Historical records show that prohibitions against same-sex acts have existed for centuries. Ancient societies, including the Assyrians and Germanic tribes, had various punishments for such acts. During the Middle Ages, European jurisdictions began adding sodomy prohibitions to secular law, often using them as a tool during times of social panic.
pages.caption: Participant carrying a poster against Section 377 during Bhubaneswar Pride Parade, India

evidence.fileTitle: File:Bhubaneswar Pride Parade 2018 02.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Participant carrying a poster against Section 377 during Bhubaneswar Pride Parade, India

pages.text: Enforcement of these laws is inherently difficult because they target private, consensual behavior. However, the existence of these laws creates a symbolic threat of state violence. This environment allows for blackmail, arbitrary arrests, and discrimination in areas like child custody and civil rights, causing severe psychological harm to LGBT individuals.
pages.caption: Proportion of the world population living in a country where homosexual acts are not criminalized, 1760–2020

evidence.fileTitle: File:Proportion of the world population living in a country where homosexual acts are not criminalized, 1760-2020.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Proportion of the world population living in a country where homosexual acts are not criminalized, 1760–2020

pages.text: Some states continue to use medically discredited anal examinations to identify homosexual activity. The United Nations considers this practice a form of torture. Currently, dozens of countries maintain laws against same-sex acts, and in at least seven nations, these acts remain punishable by death, reflecting a persistent global struggle for human rights.
